seoDesc: Thin film optics: work out optical film thickness (d) from the wavelength and the optical path difference. A free physics calculator with the formula,…
summary: Supply the wavelength, the optical path difference, the s-polarized reflectivity and the refraction angle in substrate and the Thin film optics calculator solves for optical film thickness (d). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Thin film optics calculator work?
sections.html:
The Thin film optics calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports optical film thickness (d) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the wavelength (λ), the optical path difference (OPD), the s-polarized reflectivity (Rₛ) and the refraction angle in substrate (θ₃).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Thin film optics calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Optical film thickness (d)=(1 ÷ 2) × optical path difference (OPD) ÷ (refractive index of optical film (n₂) × the cosine of (refraction angle in optical film (θ₂)))
Refractive index of optical film (n₂)=refractive index of first medium (n₁) × the sine of (incident Angle (θ₁)) ÷ the sine of (refraction angle in optical film (θ₂))
Refractive index of substrate (n₃)=refractive index of optical film (n₂) × the sine of (refraction angle in optical film (θ₂)) ÷ the sine of (refraction angle in substrate (θ₃))
Refraction angle in optical film (θ₂)=(refractive index of first medium (n₁) × (20 × the square root of (s-polarized reflectivity at first interface) − s-polarized reflectivity at first interface − 100) × the cosine of (incident Angle (θ₁)) ÷ (refractive index of optical film (n₂) × (s-polarized reflectivity at first interface − 100)))
Refraction angle in optical film (θ₂)=(refractive index of optical film (n₂) × (20 × the square root of (p-polarized reflectivity at first interface) − p-polarized reflectivity at first interface − 100) × the cosine of (incident Angle (θ₁)) ÷ (refractive index of first medium (n₁) × (p-polarized reflectivity at first interface − 100)))
Refraction angle in optical film (θ₂)=(refractive index of substrate (n₃) × (20 × the square root of (s-polarized reflectivity at second interface) − s-polarized reflectivity at second interface − 100) × the cosine of (refraction angle in substrate (θ₃)) ÷ (refractive index of optical film (n₂) × (s-polarized reflectivity at second interface − 100)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Wavelength (λ) = 0 nm, Refractive index of optical film (n₂) = 10 and Optical path difference (OPD) = 30 nm. The calculator returns Optical film thickness (d) = 1.5231 nm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Optical film thickness (d) = 1.5231 nm should be roughly the size you expected from Wavelength (λ) = 0 nm and Refractive index of optical film (n₂) = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Thin film optics calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the wavelength, the optical path difference and the s-polarized reflectivity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Thin film optics calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns optical film thickness (d), derived from the wavelength, the optical path difference and the s-polarized reflectivity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Thin film optics calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the wavelength, the optical path difference, the s-polarized reflectivity and the refraction angle in substrate, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter incident Angle (θ₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Incident Angle (θ₁) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Optical film thickness (d) = 1.5231 nm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Thin film optics calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
